Private · No tracking · Yours forever

Generating your pleasure

A personal video content management platform. Download, organize and tag your collection — then let the Arcade turn it into games built from your own library.

Get started Explore concepts Your data, your rules

Gero runs entirely on your own Windows PC. Your library, your metadata and your settings never leave it — no tracking, no analytics, no third parties.

Runs on your machine

Install it on your own Windows PC. Your videos, tags and settings stay there.

Zero tracking

No analytics, no telemetry, no cookies. Your viewing habits are yours alone.

Local storage

All videos, metadata, and settings stay on your own infrastructure.

Built-in auth

Password-protected access with secure session management.

There is one exception, and we'd rather name it than hide it: if you press Check for updates, Gero asks the supporter downloads server whether a newer version exists. It sends only your update key, nothing about you or your library, and it never happens on its own. Read the privacy policy.

How to get Gero

Simple and fair. Pay once, use forever.

Subscribe on Patreon

Subscribe to our Patreon, then log in with Patreon at the supporter downloads page. Every release is there as one version folder holding the Windows build, the Android app and the browser extensions — older versions included, plus the gameplay recordings your tier unlocks.

Once you download and install Gero, the app is yours to keep forever. Even if you cancel your subscription the next month, everything keeps working.

The only thing you miss without an active subscription are new features and updates. Want the latest and greatest? Keep your subscription active and download updates whenever they're available.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Gero is designed with privacy at its core. Your data belongs to you — always.

docs.title: Privacy first
docs.text:
Gero runs entirely on your own hardware — the Windows PC you installed it on. This means:

  • All your data stays on your own machine
  • Gero does not send your data to external servers
  • No tracking or analytics are built into the application
  • You have complete control over your installation

There is exactly one moment when Gero itself talks to a server, and you have to press a button to cause it. It is written out in full below, because a privacy promise with an unmentioned exception in it isn't worth much.

docs.title: The one exception: the update check
docs.text:
Gero can check whether a newer version of itself has been released. This is the only request Gero ever makes on its own behalf, and here is exactly what it is:

  • It only happens when you click it. The check runs when you press Check for updates in Settings → Updates, and at no other time. Gero never checks on a schedule, at startup, or in the background.
  • One server, and it's your own supporter downloads server. The request goes to the downloads page you got your key from (gero-downloads.geroappdev.workers.dev). Nowhere else.
  • It carries only the update key you pasted in yourself. Nothing else is attached. The key's only job is to prove you're a supporter.
  • It asks one question: "is there a newer version?" Nothing about your library, your tags, your videos, your settings, your installation, how you use Gero, or the machine it runs on is sent — not even the version you're currently running. The comparison with your version happens on your machine, after the answer comes back.
  • No key, no request. Without a saved update key the check cannot run at all, so if you never enter one, Gero never contacts anything.

If the answer is yes, Gero shows you the version and its release notes and waits for you to confirm. Only then does it download that release — from the same server, with the same key, and again sending nothing else.

Gero also remembers the version number and release notes locally, so it can put a quiet reminder on the homepage if you didn't install the update. That reminder is drawn from the answer you already fetched — it does not go online again.

Everything else on this page still holds without qualification: no telemetry, no analytics, no usage reporting, no crash reporting, and no background communication of any kind.

Storage of the update key

The key is stored encrypted in your own local database and is never shown back to you — the settings page only reports whether a key is set. It is only ever sent to the downloads server described above.

docs.title: What's stored locally
docs.text:
All data is stored locally:

  • Videos and media — In your configured library path
  • User accounts — Credentials are securely hashed
  • Settings — In your local database
  • Fragments and thumbnails — Stored locally
  • Metadata — Tags, actors, and video information

docs.title: We do not collect anything
docs.text:
• No usage analytics
  • No telemetry data
  • No crash or error reporting
  • No device identifiers, fingerprinting or profiling
  • No advertising trackers
  • No third-party cookies

Nothing about you, your library or how you use Gero leaves your machine. The one outbound request Gero makes — the manual update check — carries your update key and nothing else. See the one exception above.

docs.title: Third-party tools
docs.text:
Gero uses these tools locally on your own machine. The last row isn't a tool but the update check — listed here so the picture is complete:

Tool Purpose Privacy impact yt-dlp Download videos from external sources Only connects when you request a download FFmpeg Process videos All processing happens locally Ollama (optional) Local AI — frame descriptions + embeddings for the arcade games Runs on your own machine (or another PC on your network you point Gero at); nothing goes to a cloud AI service Python (opencv/librosa, optional) On-device motion + beat analysis Runs locally; only reaches out once to fetch the packages when first installed Update check (optional) Ask the supporter downloads server whether a newer Gero release exists Only runs when you press Check for updates, and only if you saved an update key; sends the key and nothing else — no library, usage or machine data

None of these ever send your videos, your metadata or your usage anywhere.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Passwords are securely hashed using industry-standard algorithms
  • Sessions are managed with secure cookies
  • HTTPS is supported via reverse proxy (recommended for remote access)
  • All data remains on your machine

docs.title: Your rights
docs.text:
Since Gero runs on your machine, you have complete control:

  • Full data ownership — Everything is yours
  • Export anytime — Back up your database and media
  • Delete anytime — Remove data or the entire application
  • Access control — Decide who can access your instance

docs.title: GDPR
docs.text:
Since Gero runs locally:

  • You are the data controller
  • You determine how data is processed
  • None of your content, metadata or usage is shared with us (the software developers)

The only thing that ever reaches us is your update key, and only in the moment you press Check for updates. It tells the downloads server that a valid supporter asked for the current version number. You can stop even that by removing the key in Settings → Updates.

docs.title: Arcade: Caption Creator
docs.text:
Caption Creator lets you compose a multi-clip story from your library and have an AI write captions that match what's on screen — turning a sequence of fragments into a narrated, captioned mini-story.

Experimental — use at your own risk

The AI side of Caption Creator has only just been integrated and is not fully tested yet. It works reasonably well, but expect rough edges. The tag timeline and frame description features described below are in-progress concepts that are still being refined. Nothing here can damage your library, but results will vary.

docs.title: What is Caption Creator?
docs.text:
You build a story out of clips from your library and arrange them in order. For each clip, an AI language model writes a caption that fits the visuals. The result is a captioned story you can play back.

The AI needs two kinds of understanding to do this well:

  1. What's in each frame — produced by a vision model that tags the frames of your clips (see Frame tagging).
  2. How to write the caption — produced by a text model that turns those visual facts into a caption.

Both run locally through Ollama. Nothing is sent to a cloud service.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install and run Ollama
docs.text:
Install Ollama on a machine that GERO can reach over HTTP (your own PC, or another machine on your network). By default Ollama listens on http://localhost:11434.

Pull three models — a text model, a vision model, and an embedding model:

# TEXT — writes the captions (pick one your hardware can run)
ollama pull llama3.1

# VISION — looks at your clips and describes each frame. JoyCaption is purpose-built for detailed,
# natural descriptions and gives the best "Describe all videos" results:
ollama pull aha2025/llama-joycaption-beta-one-hf-llava:Q5_K_M
#   ↳ Q5_K_M is a good balance; Q4_K_M is lighter, Q6_K / Q8_0 are heavier + sharper. A general
#     vision model like llava also works as a fallback:  ollama pull llava

# EMBEDDING — turns those descriptions into vectors for clip matching. nomic-embed-text is the tried-
# and-tested choice:
ollama pull nomic-embed-text

The AI models power the library-wide content matching

The Describe pass (vision model) and the embeddings it produces (embedding model) drive the smart clip-matching across the arcade. Caption Creator and QuizTime match clips by embedding similarity — they need both a vision and an embedding model. Follow the Beat is different: it matches on motion tempo + your tag/actor filter only, so it needs no AI models at all. See Local analysis tools for the motion side (Python), which pairs with this.

Hardware matters

Larger models produce better captions but need more RAM/VRAM and run slower. Start with a smaller model, confirm the flow works, then scale up.

docs.title: Step 2 — Point GERO at Ollama
docs.text:
In GERO, go to Settings → AI provider and:

  1. Set the provider to Ollama
  2. Add a server with the base URL of your Ollama instance (e.g. http://localhost:11434)
  3. Tick the capabilities that server should handle — text, vision, and/or embed. You can split these across multiple machines if you have them
  4. Choose the default story model (the text model that writes captions)

If GERO can reach the server, the model dropdowns fill in automatically from what Ollama has pulled. If it can't reach it, you'll get a free-text box instead — double-check the URL and that Ollama is running.

docs.title: Step 3 — Configure frame tagging
docs.text:
Go to Settings → Frame tagging. This controls the "Analyze frames" job, which is how GERO understands the visuals of your clips:

  • Vision model — the Ollama vision model that tags each sampled frame
  • Tag vocabulary — whether the model may only pick from a video's own tags, or from all tags
  • Frame resolution / interval — how large each sampled frame is, and how often frames are sampled. Denser sampling is more accurate but slower

The per-frame tags this job produces become the visual context the caption model reads.

docs.title: In-progress concepts
docs.text:
These are the experimental knobs being used to push caption quality. They live under Settings → Arcade (Caption Creator) and Settings → AI provider, and their behaviour may change between releases.

Concept What it does Frame description (detailed beats) Feeds the caption model a per-frame breakdown of each clip, so captions can reference what happens moment to moment rather than just the clip as a whole. Can be limited to shorter clips to keep prompts manageable. Tag timeline Feeds the model a per-second timeline of which tags are active, giving it a sense of timing — when something starts, peaks, and ends within a clip. Time pins Lets the model anchor a caption to an exact second in a clip.

These are deliberately experimental. If captions come out odd, try toggling them off and regenerating.

docs.title: Using Caption Creator
docs.text:
1. Create a level — pick the clips for your story and arrange them in order
  2. Analyze frames — run frame tagging so the AI knows what's in each clip
  3. Generate captions — the text model writes a caption per clip from the visual context
  4. Review and tweak — edit any caption by hand; regenerate individual clips as needed
  5. Play — run the level to see your story with its captions

It's a starting point

Caption Creator is the newest game in GERO and the AI behind it is early. Treat generated captions as a draft you refine, not a finished product — and expect this whole flow to get noticeably better over the next releases.

docs.title: Arcade: Dare deck
docs.text:
Dare deck is the hands-off game in Gero's Arcade. You pick a mode, pick how long each line stays on screen, and press play. From there it runs on its own — a compilation video with a line of text over it, one after another, until it tells you what you're left with.

There is nothing to click during a round. That's the point.

docs.title: What is Dare deck?
docs.text:
Every round is built the same way:

  1. An intro card names the mode and tells you how many options are coming
  2. Each option plays in turn — one line of text, held over a fullscreen feed of clips from your library
  3. An outro card asks you the question the mode was built around

What changes between modes is when you commit to an option, and what the line means once you have.

No AI required

Dare deck runs entirely on content that ships with Gero — 2,000 written lines, seeded into your database on first start. No Ollama, no model, no setup. It works on a fresh install with nothing but videos in your library.

docs.title: The six modes
docs.text: Mode How you choose Options Draws from Choose your fate Watch all of them, then commit 3, 5 or 7 Fates Left or right Pick a side before anything plays Always 2 Statements Pick a number Call a number before the reveal 3, 5 or 7 Statements Count your yes Answer every one silently, tally at the end 5, 10 or 15 Questions Last one standing You don't — the deck decides 3, 5 or 7 Fates Your week You don't — every day gets one 5 or 7 Day rules

docs.title: Choose your fate
docs.text: Each option is a fate: an outcome with a consequence attached, not a task. Every one of them plays out in full, labelled A through to the last letter, and only when they've all been shown do you say which one was yours.

docs.title: Left or right
docs.text: Two options, and you pick your side before either has played. Both are shown — first the left, then the right — and the outro tells you which one you just committed to. Binary, blind and short.

docs.title: Pick a number
docs.text: The same blind commitment, but you call a number between 1 and the option count first. The numbers are shown large; the reveal decides the rest.

docs.title: Count your yes
docs.text: Instead of picking one line, you answer all of them — yes or no, in your head, honestly. At the outro you tap your tally on a 0-to-n picker and get a verdict scaled to how many you said yes to, so the closing line reads the same whether you played 5 questions or 15.

docs.title: Last one standing
docs.text:
Every fate plays out, and then the deck starts crossing them off — one every six seconds — until a single one is left. That one is yours, and you had no say in it.

Tip

The strike order is decided when the round is composed, not while it plays. Refreshing the page mid-cull won't reshuffle who survives.

docs.title: Your week
docs.text: One rule per day, pinned to Monday through to the end of the week. These are day-long conditions rather than single acts — obligations, prohibitions, repetitions, counts — and the outro hands you the whole week at once as a schedule.

docs.title: A voice per mode
docs.text:
Each mode sets its lines in its own typeface, so the same layout reads differently depending on what you're playing:

Mode Face Choose your fate Playfair Display, italic Left or right Bebas Neue, caps Pick a number Cinzel, caps Count your yes Space Grotesk Last one standing Archivo Black Your week Zilla Slab

Numbers always opt out of the mode face and use a plain system font — a display serif is the wrong tool for a grid of digits.

docs.title: The clip feed
docs.text:
Behind every line, Gero plays a fullscreen feed built from your library: the strongest matches for that line, back to back, for as long as the line is on screen. There are always enough clips queued to fill the time limit without repeating one immediately.

Clips are letterboxed rather than cropped, so portrait footage keeps its full frame.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The start screen is two steps — pick a mode, then pick your setting and play:

Setting Options Default Option count Depends on the mode (see the table above) 5 (10 for Count your yes, 7 for Your week) Seconds per line 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 30

Two more live in the options panel and are remembered between sessions:

Option Description Pause key Rebindable key that pauses and resumes a round. Defaults to Space Ignore videos with tag Any tag listed here is kept out of the clip feed entirely

docs.title: The written content
docs.text:
Four pools ship with Gero, 500 lines each:

Pool Used by Lines Fates Choose your fate, Last one standing 500 Statements Left or right, Pick a number 500 Questions Count your yes 500 Day rules Your week 500

Gero records how often each line has been drawn and prefers the ones you've seen least, so the pool works its way through before anything comes back around.

The intro and outro cards are written per mode too — ten variants each — and one is picked per session, so a replay of the same mode never opens with the same words.
