docs.title: Arcade: Follow the Beat
docs.text: Follow the Beat is one of Gero's Arcade games — a rhythm-based experience where your video clips play in sync with a music track, transitioning on the beat. Its headline trick: point it at a song and Gero auto-fills the whole video for you, matching clips from your library to the beat.

docs.title: What is Follow the Beat?
docs.text:
Pick a song, let Gero analyze the beats (or map them yourself), and watch your video fragments play in perfect rhythm with the music. Fragments transition on beat, visual effects pulse with the rhythm, and timed instructions appear at key moments.

It supports 1 to 3 video screens playing simultaneously, each with its own timeline and fragment sequence.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a level — Each level is built around a specific audio track with a beat profile
  2. Beats are analyzed — Gero auto-detects the BPM and beat positions, or you set them manually
  3. Auto-fill from the beat — Gero matches clips from your library to the song by their measured motion tempo — from the pool your content filter allows (tags, actors, …) — and lays them across the timeline locked to the beat (each clip is speed-adjusted so its motion lands on the rhythm). You can still place or tweak clips by hand
  4. Fragments play in sync — Video clips transition on beat markers across one or more screens
  5. Visual effects — An optional theme is applied to all video screens (grayscale, neon, glitch, etc.)
  6. Timed instructions — Text overlays appear at specific timestamps with animations
  7. Completion — When the song ends, a completion screen shows with an optional custom message

docs.title: Level editor
docs.text: The level editor gives you full control over every aspect of a Follow the Beat level.

docs.title: Auto-fill from the beat
docs.text:
This is the fast way to build a level. Hit Auto-fill on a screen and Gero fills its timeline for you:

  • It splits the song into beat-timed sections and, for each, picks a clip whose measured motion tempo locks to that section's beat — calm parts get calm footage, drops get high-energy footage.
  • Clips are drawn only from what your content filter allows (tags, actors, subscriptions, duration, …), so the footage stays on-theme.
  • Each clip is speed-adjusted so its motion lands on the rhythm, and no clip is reused, so the result stays varied.

You can auto-fill a whole screen, or fill only the gaps around clips you've already placed, then fine-tune by hand.

Auto-fill needs Analyse motion

Auto-fill picks clips by their motion tempo, so run Analyse motion on your videos first (see Local analysis tools (Python)) — without motion profiles there's nothing in the pool to match. That's the only prerequisite: matching is motion + your filter, so Follow the Beat needs no AI models (no vision model, no embeddings — unlike Caption Creator).

docs.title: Audio track
docs.text:
• Track selection — Browse your audio library and pick a track
  • Beat profile — View and edit BPM, first beat offset, and individual beat markers
  • Auto-analysis — Let Gero detect beats automatically, or map them manually
  • Speed segments — Define time ranges with custom playback speeds (0.5x to 2.0x) on a dedicated visual band

docs.title: Timeline editor
docs.text:
The timeline is the core of the level editor. It shows the full level duration with beat markers overlaid.

  • Screen bands — One lane per video screen (up to 3). Each lane shows its segments
  • Media segments — Drag a specific fragment or video onto the timeline. Supports trim offset for starting partway through
  • Filter segments — Drag a filter block onto the timeline; at play time Gero fills it live with clips matching the filter. (For a baked, motion-matched result instead, use Auto-fill above.)
  • Snap to beat — Segments snap to beat markers when dragged or resized
  • Cross-band snapping — Segments also snap to edges of segments on other bands. Guide lines appear during drag operations
  • Resize — Drag segment edges to make them longer or shorter
  • Double-click — Expands a segment to fill available space
  • Right-click — Delete a segment
  • Copy / paste — Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V to duplicate segments

docs.title: Fragment filters
docs.text:
Each filter segment can have its own criteria:

Filter Description Tags Include or exclude tags. Supports AND/OR matching Actors Include or exclude actors (with profile photo previews) Subscriptions Filter by media subscription source Duration Minimum and maximum fragment duration in seconds Source type URL, file, or recording Media type All, fragments only, or videos only Review status Reviewed, unreviewed, or any

docs.title: Visual effects
docs.text:
Apply a visual theme to the entire level:

Effect Description None No effect applied Grayscale Black and white Sepia Warm brown tone Blue overlay Blue color grading Vignette Darkened edges Scanlines Retro TV scanline effect Glitch RGB color shifting Anime Enhanced colors and contrast Neon High saturation glow

docs.title: Beat animations
docs.text:
Each screen can have its own beat animation that triggers on every beat:

  • Bounce — Screen bounces on beat
  • Shake — Screen shakes horizontally
  • Pulse — Screen scales up and down
  • Vibrate — Rapid micro-shake

docs.title: Fragment transitions
docs.text:
Choose how fragments transition between each other:

  • Crossfade
  • Bounce in
  • Fade in
  • Swipe left / swipe right
  • Zoom in
  • Slide up

docs.title: Timed instructions
docs.text:
Add text overlays that appear at specific timestamps during the level:

  • Timing — Set start and end times (or duration)
  • Text — Supports markdown formatting
  • Entry animation — Fade in, slide up/down, bounce in, zoom in
  • Exit animation — Fade out, slide down
  • Loop animation — Pulse, float, glitch, glow, shake, typewriter
  • Styling — Color, font size, font family, bold, italic, underline
  • Position — Top, center, or bottom of the screen
  • Alignment — Left, center, or right

docs.title: Gameplay controls
docs.text: Key Action Space Pause / resume M Mute / unmute audio ESC Quit game (with confirmation)

docs.title: Bot recordings
docs.text: Follow the Beat levels can be recorded automatically using the bot system. The bot plays the level in a headless browser with frame-by-frame capture, producing a video file. Useful for creating preview videos or promotional content.

docs.title: Arcade: Obey
docs.text: Obey is the guided session game in Gero's Arcade. You pick a persona, a length and an intensity, and she runs the whole thing: a scripted story told one order at a time, over a feed of clips from your library, using the toys you have catalogued as products. You don't build anything — you confirm, you wait out a countdown, and you do as you're told.

docs.title: What a session is
docs.text:
A session is generated in full the moment you start it, then played back stage by stage. Nothing is improvised mid-run — the story, the props, the outcome and the running order are all decided up front, which is why a session survives a page refresh.

  1. A prep screen — "You'll need all of this" lists every outfit piece, prop and item the session will call for, so you can lay them out first
  2. The doll-up — always the first stage: she has you put the entire look on, and confirm
  3. The story — the chapters of one story arc, one order per stage
  4. The finale — three escalating beats around a hold, then the climax reveal
  5. Aftercare — a closing stage, then the report

The report tells you how many commands you obeyed out of the total, her closing mood, and which of the two endings you got.

docs.title: The personas
docs.text:
Five personas ship with Gero. Only the first is free; the rest are unlocked with coins earned by playing. Each has her own portrait, voice, tastes and intensity band.

Persona Unlock Reaches She's into Mistress Vell Free Soft – Firm Dress-up, tease, worship, oral Domina Rae 150 coins Teasing – Harsh Denial, toys, discipline, anal Lady Noir 300 coins Teasing – Harsh Exposure, dress-up, tease, big toys The Warden 500 coins Firm – Merciless Chastity, denial, endurance, anal Mistress Onyx 800 coins Firm – Merciless Big toys, gape, endurance, exposure

Each persona also has a signature woven into every session she runs, regardless of which story comes up — Vell always starts at the mirror, Rae counts every edge out loud, The Warden locks you in a cage during the doll-up and only hands the key back if she lets you finish. Personas are fixed; you cannot create or edit them.

docs.title: Profiles and setup
docs.text:
Everything you earn belongs to a profile, not to your account. A profile holds its own coins, unlocked personas and bond levels, and its name is what she calls you during play. You can keep several and delete any of them to start over. Once you pick a persona, the setup sheet asks for two things:

Setting Options Default How long 10m, 20m, 30m, 45m 20m Intensity Soft, Teasing, Firm, Harsh, Merciless The highest tier she currently allows

The intensity list is capped by your bond with that persona, not by the persona alone. She starts one tier above her floor and allows one more tier per bond level until her own ceiling is reached.

Naming a profile Admin

A profile named Admin is the tester profile: every persona is unlocked, the full intensity range is available, and a Skip button appears on every stage.

docs.title: The story arcs
docs.text:
Six story arcs are written into Gero. One is picked per session, weighted by how well its themes overlap the persona's interests — so The Warden keeps landing on chastity stories without ever being locked to them.

Arc Runs on Dolled up & plugged Anal, dress-up, tease, toys The lockup Chastity and denial The exhibition Exposure and performance Good girl training Obedience and verbal work Stretched Big toys, gape, endurance At her service Service and worship

An arc is a sequence of chapters, each with a title that shows on screen as the stage label. Every chapter position offers a few alternative orders and one is rolled per session, so the same arc plays differently each time. Arcs also carry props — a plug, a large toy — bound to one real product at the start and then referred to for the rest of the session: the plug from chapter two is the same plug she asks to see in chapter six.

The doll-up always includes panties, a bra, a skirt or dress, makeup, lipstick and a wig; stockings, lashes, earrings, piercings and heels roll in and out. Clothing can be taken off later in the story — makeup, jewellery and the wig stay on throughout.

The session outcome — whether she lets you finish or denies you — is decided at roughly even odds before the first stage and only revealed at the climax.

docs.title: Orders and pacing
docs.text:
There are three kinds of stage:

  • Timed orders — an instruction with a countdown. You press I have it · Start when you're ready, the timer runs, and Done appears when it hits zero. The last five seconds are counted down large on screen.
  • Confirm-only stages — no timer. The doll-up and the wardrobe changes just wait for you to press Obey.
  • Choices — she asks a question and you pick an answer. These are interludes: they carry no timer and don't count toward your command total.

Pacing is fitted to the length you chose: the build-up gets about 70% of it and the finale takes the rest. If the story doesn't fit, optional chapters are dropped first, then lower-priority ones — the core of the arc and her signature are never cut. Whatever room is left is spread evenly across the timed stages, so a 10-minute session plays the same story at its quickest and a 45-minute one plays it unhurried.

Your answers to choice beats move her mood between soft and hard, shown on screen as "She's easing off" through "She's riled up". Mood then re-picks the next tradeable stage toward a milder or hotter alternative from the same story position.

You get one swap per session (more with a skill), which re-rolls the current order into a sibling alternative, keeping the story and its props intact. Wardrobe stages, choices, the finale, aftercare and anything on the story's spine can't be swapped, and the button hides itself when that's the case. The Stop button is the safeword: one press ends the session immediately, with no confirmation.

docs.title: Her voice
docs.text:
Every order and every praise line can be spoken aloud. Gero generates the audio per stage with Piper, a local text-to-speech engine, using the voice model assigned to that persona — Vell speaks with en_US-amy-medium, The Warden with the flat, low en_US-kathleen-low, Onyx with the Scottish en_GB-alba-medium, and so on.

Voice needs Piper installed

Piper and the persona voice models are not bundled with the app. Out of the box the Piper executable and voice model paths are empty, and Obey runs text-only until you point them at an installed Piper. Nothing breaks — she simply stays silent, no error is shown, and the session plays exactly the same. If a persona's assigned voice model isn't installed, Gero falls back to the first voice it can find.

Personas can also be given an optional Ollama text model that rephrases each seeded line in her own voice before it's spoken. No persona ships with one configured, so by default she speaks the written line verbatim. If a model is set but Ollama is unreachable, the original line is used.

docs.title: The clip feed
docs.text:
Behind every order, Gero plays a continuous fullscreen feed of clips from your library, chosen to fit what she's telling you to do.

Matching works in three passes. First it looks at your videos' cached frame descriptions, ranking them by how many of the stage's keywords — the item terms she's naming, plus the stage's theme tags — appear in what the frames were described as showing. If nothing matches, it falls back to a tag and title match, and finally to any playable video.

The previous stage's clips are pushed to the back of the queue so the background changes when the order does; if an embedding model is configured, the remaining candidates are additionally sorted most-different-first. Clips are letterboxed rather than cropped, and play muted unless you turn clip sound on.

docs.title: Products and toys
docs.text:
Obey draws on your product catalogue. When the story calls for a plug, a wand or a pair of heels, Gero matches that slot against your product category names and aliases and picks a real product from the matches — with its photo, shown as a reference chip beside the order and in the prep list. She never says the product's name: the instruction always uses the generic term ("your little plug", "your wand"), and the real name only labels the chip on screen. Within a session, no product is picked twice.

Products are optional

If a slot matches no category, or every product in it is already in use, the order keeps its generic wording and shows no chip. The session runs fine on an empty catalogue — you just lose the photos and the "use this one" specificity.

docs.title: Settings and controls
docs.text:
The options sheet is shared across every persona and profile:

Setting Description Default Clip sound Play the gameplay clip with its own audio Off Her voice She speaks her commands aloud On Next stage key Rebindable key that starts or confirms an order Space Pause key Rebindable key that pauses and resumes Escape Excluded tags Videos with these tags never appear in Obey None

Pausing stops the clip, the voice and the countdown together. Excluded tags are global — they apply to every persona and every profile.

docs.title: Coins, bond and skills
docs.text:
Finishing a session pays the active profile 50 coins plus 5 per command obeyed, and adds 5 affinity plus 1 per command to your bond with that persona. Every 40 affinity is one bond level, and each level lets her go one intensity tier further.

Coins unlock new personas and buy per-persona skills:

Skill Cost Requires Effect Second thoughts 120 coins — One extra swap every session Sharper edge 250 coins Bond lv 1 She'll push you one tier harder Insatiable 500 coins Bond lv 3 She goes two tiers beyond her usual reach

Skills are bought from the setup sheet and belong to one persona on one profile. The tier bonuses don't stack — the strongest one you own applies.

docs.title: Arcade: QuizTime
docs.text: QuizTime is the first game in Gero's Arcade — a mode that transforms your media collection into interactive experiences. Instead of just watching, you play.

docs.title: What is QuizTime?
docs.text:
QuizTime is a multiple-choice quiz game where questions are displayed over video backgrounds from your library. Answer questions, earn points, and trigger challenges based on your score.

Think of it as a trivia game powered entirely by your own content.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a level — Each level is a set of questions with its own theme and settings
  2. Questions appear — A question is shown on screen with multiple answer options
  3. Video backgrounds — While you answer, relevant video fragments play behind the question
  4. Earn points — Each answer has a point value. Some answers give more points than others
  5. Trigger challenges — Certain answers or score thresholds can trigger special challenges
  6. End screen — See your final score with a custom message based on how well you did

docs.title: Level configuration
docs.text: Each QuizTime level is fully configurable:

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
• Question text — The prompt shown to the player
  • Instructions — Optional detailed instructions (supports markdown)
  • Answers — 2-4 answer options, each with a point value
  • Background filter — Which video fragments to play during this question (filtered by tags)
  • Video screen count — Show 1, 2, or 3 video screens simultaneously

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Description Time limit Optional timer per question (seconds) Show points on answers Display point values on the answer buttons Theme Visual style (Normal, Fast and Furious, Sex on the Beach, Dark and Stormy) Fragment transition Animation between video clips (e.g., Crossfade)

docs.title: End screen
docs.text:
• None — Game just ends
  • Custom — Show a fixed message
  • Score-based — Different messages depending on your score (e.g., "Great job!" above 80%, "Try again!" below 50%)

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
Challenges are special actions triggered during gameplay:

  • Answer triggers — Selecting a specific answer activates a challenge
  • Score triggers — Reaching a score threshold activates a challenge

Challenges can use fragment filters to select specific video content, making each playthrough feel different based on your library.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Default key bindings during gameplay:

Key Action 1, 2, 3, 4 Select answer 1-4 M Mute/unmute

docs.title: Audio settings
docs.text:
• Background music — Toggle on/off, adjust volume (0-100)
  • Fragment audio — Toggle video audio on/off, adjust volume (0-100)

docs.title: Other arcade games
docs.text:
QuizTime is one of several games in Gero's Arcade, with more planned:

Game Description Status Follow the Beat Auto-built beat-synced video from your library Available Caption Creator Multi-clip stories with AI-written captions Available QuizTime Multiple-choice quiz with video backgrounds Available OnlyCams Build a camming career Available Flamr Swipe to rate and curate your library, Tinder-style Available Dare deck Six hands-off modes over a compilation feed Available To cum or not to cum A night at the fair — tickets, challenges and a gamble Available Obey A timed, narrated session Available Find the Clip Identify the correct video clip Planned Tell Me a Story Narrative game with text and audio Planned

The level-based games (QuizTime, Follow the Beat, Caption Creator) share the same level and challenge system, so you can build and share content packs for them.

docs.title: Arcade: To cum or not to cum
Arcade: To cum or not to cum
docs.text:
To cum or not to cum (game type to-cum-or-not-to-cum) is a night at the fair. You watch clips from your own library, every clip you sit out pays tickets, and you spend those tickets at four booths on the midway wheel — a new channel, a spin of the mystery wheel, a lucky charm from the trinket stand, or a gamble on how the night ends.

The game is levelless: a single public level, Main stage (slug main-stage), is seeded so sessions have something to attach to. All rules run in the browser; the backend engine only stores the latest snapshot and closes the session on the final outcome.

docs.title: The night loop
docs.text:
1. Pick a difficulty — sets every price, how fast your multiplier grows, and the odds at the finish booth
  2. Pick a channel — the first pick is free and cannot be cancelled
  3. Watch — clips play full screen; watched time pays tickets into the hub of the midway wheel
  4. Spend at the midway — change channel, spin the wheel, buy a trinket, or try to finish
  5. The night ends — the finish booth decides whether you win, lose, or keep going

Every booth, stand and reveal is a menu over the clips, and opening one pauses every screen; the clips pick up where they left off when you close it.

docs.title: Difficulties
docs.text:
Picked once, before the night starts, and shown in the top rail for the rest of the run.

Difficulty Tagline Channel Wheel Finish Trinkets 1st multiplier step Later steps Princess A gentle night — the fair adores you 40 150 1200 ×0.75 +1.0 +0.5 Good girl The house standard — fair but firm 60 200 2000 ×1 +0.5 +0.25 Slut The night gets expensive for girls like you 100 300 3000 ×1.5 +0.5 +0.25 Whore Everything costs. Nothing is given 150 450 5000 ×2.25 +0.25 +0.25

Good girl is the default. Harder modes also get worse odds at the finish booth (see below). The trinket column is the factor applied to every charm's list price, rounded to a tenner.

docs.title: Earning tickets
docs.text:
• Watched time is worth 1 ticket per 5 seconds (per 4 or 3 with the pocket watch), plus a flat 1 ticket for reaching the end of the clip (2 or 3 with the ticket punch).
  • Tickets are only handed over when a clip is watched out. A clip you skip halfway pays nothing.
  • The last stretch of watched time and the completion bonus are handed over as one payout, so the number printed on the stub is exactly what lands on the counter.
  • Long clips pay along the way, in blocks of 30 watched seconds — but a block is only split off when more than 10 seconds are still to come, so a short tail always rides along on the final payout.
  • Only forward playback counts. Scrubbing, pausing or looping back never mints tickets.
  • Every payout is multiplied by your current multiplier (and by the golden-clip factor), then flies from the screen that won it to the counter as a ticket stub.

docs.title: Golden clips
docs.text: Each clip has a 5% chance of being golden (12% once you own the rabbit's foot). A golden clip is dressed with a gold frame, corner glints and a "Golden clip — pays ×5 · watch it out" banner, and pays ×5 for as long as it runs.

docs.title: The multiplier
docs.text: You start at ×1. The only way it grows is by accepting a challenge from the mystery wheel: the first accepted challenge adds your difficulty's first step, every one after that adds the smaller step. It never goes back down — not even when the finish wheel burns your tickets. Denying a challenge changes nothing; the tickets you paid for the spin are already spent.

docs.title: The mystery wheel
docs.text:
Buying a spin plays a wheel animation, then presents a challenge card with Accept and Deny. Per bought spin you get one re-spin at half price (rounded up, and free with the lucky horseshoe), before you decide.

The wheel remembers what it already gave you: a challenge that has come up is held back until every other challenge in the pool has come up once, and only then does the cycle start over. So no repeats back to back, and a re-spin can never hand you the same card again.

Every challenge in the pool has the same chance of coming up. The only rule that narrows the pool is dress/undress: a dress challenge can only appear when you are not already dressed by an earlier challenge, an undress challenge only when you are.

Wheel label What it asks Draws from your products Use a toy Use it on yourself while the clips keep rolling Toys Change position Move to a named position and stay there — never the same one twice in a row — Dress up Dress up before the next clip ends (dress) Clothing Lingerie time Put lingerie on and let the screens see it (dress) Lingerie Doll up A complete named look, head to toe, nothing skipped (dress) See outfit templates Get naked Strip, everything off, before the next clip ends (undress) — Make up Put on make up, take your time — Go outside Go outside for a few seconds, exactly as you are — Sloppy blowjob Give a dildo a sloppy blowjob Small / medium / large dildo Catwalk run Put the shoes on and do a catwalk run across the room Shoes Follow along Act exactly like the person in the next clip — Record yourself Record yourself for the rest of the clip — Prettiest moan Practice your prettiest moan along with the next clip — Spank yourself Spank yourself after every clip that ends — Edge once Edge once before the next clip ends, then hands off —

The positions drawn by Change position are: cowgirl, doggy, standing doggy, reverse cowgirl, on your back, on your belly, on your side.

Product challenges need a stocked collection

Challenges that draw from products resolve to a real item from your collection, matched by category (sub-categories count too), and show its photo and name on the card. If the category is empty, the challenge still comes up — it just falls back to generic wording ("a toy from your collection", "your highest heels"). Fill in your products to get concrete instructions.

docs.title: Outfit templates
docs.text: Doll up picks one pre-composed look and dresses it slot by slot, so the pieces always go together. The ten templates are schoolgirl, pole dancer, office lady, night out, boudoir, beach day, latex doll, casual day, bedtime and showgirl. Each slot (wig, lipstick, bra, heels, …) is filled with a real, non-repeated item from your collection where one exists; slots your collection cannot fill are left to you.

docs.title: The booths
docs.text:
There is no bar along the bottom any more. The whole midway is one wheel in the bottom-right corner: a brass rim of chasing bulbs, a wedge per booth, and your ticket count in the hub. A wedge you can afford lights up; the moment one opens the rim gives a tick, so a booth announces itself by moving rather than by hanging a sign over the clip.

Clicking the wheel spins it and throws the midway open across the screen — four lit booths side by side under a striped awning, each dropping in on its own beat. Pick one and it opens; the wheel closes behind you.

Booth What it does Channel Re-opens the channel booth and switches the program Wheel Buys one spin of the mystery wheel Trinkets Opens the trinket stand — lucky charms that keep working Finish Gambles everything on the verdict — to cum, or not to cum

Walking up to the trinket stand is free; it charges per charm instead. Its wedge quotes the cheapest thing you could still buy there, and reads "Sold out" once every charm is yours.

The wheel is shuttered while an overlay is open, while paused, and during the victory lap.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channels are your theater presets: a name, a screen count and one content filter per screen (tags, actors, and everything else a theater filter holds). Up to 4 screens play at once; presets with more are clamped. Only the first screen carries sound.

There is always a free-for-all option, The whole fair — one screen, unfiltered.

A dark channel is free to leave

If every screen in the picked channel comes up empty, the booth re-opens at no cost and without a cancel button. Picking a channel also resets each screen's playhead, since a new channel is a new feed.

docs.title: The trinket stand
docs.text:
Everything else at the fair is spent the moment you buy it. A trinket keeps working for the rest of the night. Most are bought once; two have a second rung you can come back for.

Trinket Price (Good girl) What it does Brass ticket punch 350 · 700 Watching a clip out pays 2 instead of 1, and 3 at the second rung Rabbit's foot 300 Golden clips go from 5% to 12% Lucky horseshoe 400 The wheel's re-spin is free instead of half price Bingo card 450 25 tags that tick themselves as you watch Insurance slip 500 The next Denied burns half your tickets instead of all of them — then the slip burns too Brass pocket watch 600 · 900 Watched time pays a ticket every 4 seconds instead of 5, and every 3 at the second rung

Prices scale with the difficulty (see the difficulty table). A charm you already own shows the rung you are on and what the next one would do; the insurance slip is the only one that is used up, and once it has saved you the stand will sell you another.

docs.title: Trying to finish
docs.text:
Buying a finish spends the tickets up front and reveals one weighted verdict. With the spyglass an odds sheet comes first, and you can still walk away without paying. The weights depend on the difficulty (they add up to 100, so read them as percentages).

Verdict What happens Princess Good girl Slut Whore Denied Your tickets drop to 0 (half, with an insurance slip), your multiplier stays, the night rolls on 20 30 35 40 No cum. Bad luck The night ends, unfinished — game over 5 10 12 15 To cum You win — on to the cooldown 30 20 15 10 To cum… and lick it up You win, with one last task — on to the cooldown 15 15 13 10 To cum… and use it as lube Go ahead, but the night continues and the counter keeps running 15 15 15 15 Only if you can sissygasm in 5 minutes A 5-minute countdown starts over the still-playing clips 15 10 10 10

The sissygasm verdict shows a countdown with an I did it button. Pressing it wins the night; letting the clock run out is a game over. The deadline is stored as a timestamp, so refreshing does not buy you extra time.

docs.title: Cooldown and the end screen
docs.text: A won night lands in the cooldown phase: the screens keep playing for as long as you want, the ticket counter is frozen, and a slim banner offers Leave the fair. Leaving shows the end screen, which comes in two flavours — completed (gold) and game over (dark). Both list tickets earned, clips watched, challenges accepted and your final multiplier, with Play again and Back to the arcade.

docs.title: Resuming a night
docs.text: Every change to the run is written to browser storage, including the difficulty, tickets, multiplier, channel, the playhead of each screen, the charms you bought, the challenges the wheel already used and any running sissygasm deadline. Close the tab or refresh and the front gate offers Resume your night instead of Step right up; the screens pick up on the clip they were on rather than replaying from the top. Finished nights are cleared, so they always start over, and New game on the menu discards a saved run — and its tickets — on the spot.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Input Action Space (configurable) Pause / resume the clips ESC Open / close the quit dialog Arrow down / arrow up Next / previous clip (an unfinished clip pays nothing) Arrow right / arrow left Scrub 5 seconds forward / back inside the running clip Scroll or swipe up/down Reel through the clips on that screen

The top rail mirrors the transport buttons and adds mute, panic mode and leaving the fair.

docs.title: Hiding a clip
docs.text: Every screen carries a hide button in its bottom-right corner, the same one theater has and doing the same thing: the clip is hidden from your library and the reel moves straight on. Hiding a video hides its fragments with it, exactly as in theater. You were never going to watch it out, so it pays nothing.

docs.title: The bingo card
docs.text:
Bought at the trinket stand, the card hangs along the bottom edge of the screen for the rest of the night: cream stock, a red BINGO banner across the head, and 25 tags drawn from the ones you use most.

Every clip that plays daubs whatever tags it matches — you never click anything. A completed row or column pays, the full card pays a lot more, and each line pays only once. Fold the card away with the chevron in the banner when you would rather see the clip.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Two options, saved as user settings on the backend:

Setting Description Sound on by default How every new night starts. You can still mute in-game Pause key The key that pauses and resumes the clips. Default Space; press the button and hit a key to rebind, Escape cancels

Content filtering lives in the channel

There are no tag or actor filters on the settings screen — what you see is decided by the channel you pick, which is a theater preset with its own filters per screen. Build the presets you want in theater and they show up in the channel booth.

docs.title: Arcade: Toy tester
docs.text:
Toy tester (game type toy-tester) is a shop you run. Brands write to you offering a product from your own catalogue to test; you film the review on your webcam, and the product then sits on one of your shelves for a few days, selling to customers and paying you a commission. That commission buys more shelves, a bigger cut and campaigns.

Listings expire, so a shop you stop filming for slowly empties out. That is the pressure the whole game runs on.

Unlike the other arcade games, this one is a save, not a run: the shop lives on the server and is still there next time. You can keep several shops side by side.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Open the shop — nothing has moved since you left; the day only ends when you say so
  2. Read the offers — a brand, a product, a brief and a fee
  3. Take it or leave it — turning an offer down costs standing; paying the kill fee does not
  4. Film the test — the webcam records while you work through the brief
  5. Price it — the listing goes up at whatever you ask
  6. Sell — the next time you open the shop, that listing pays out
  7. Spend — shelves, your cut, or the size of the shop itself

docs.title: Shops and the test shop
docs.text:
You can run more than one shop. Each keeps its own money, shelves, inbox, standing and history. Click the shop name at the top of the shop to get back to the picker, where you switch between shops, open another or delete one. Switching closes the books on the shop you switch to, exactly as opening one does.

Deleting a shop takes its shelves, its archive and every review you filmed for it — the video files are removed from storage, not just the entries. You can delete your last shop; you simply land back on the picker with nothing open.

A brand new shop starts with 120 in the bank, three empty shelves and standing 50, which is worth four offers waiting in the inbox straight away. No receipt prints on that first visit — there is nothing to settle yet.

A shop named admin is a test shop

Name the tester admin when creating a shop and it opens with every upgrade already bought, maximum standing and a balance you cannot spend through. It exists so the whole game can be reached without playing up to it, and it works on any install — unlike a dev-only endpoint, which is what OnlyCams uses.

docs.title: Offers
docs.text:
What gets tested is always a toy. Offers are drawn from the Toys group of your catalogue — the dildos, the plugs, the chastity cages, the vibrators. The rest of your catalogue is not ignored; it turns up as extras on the brief. Products already on a shelf or already in the inbox are never offered again while they are there, so the same item is never in front of you twice.

An offer carries one job and one to three extras:

  • The job follows from what kind of toy it is. A plug gets asked to go in and out five times, or to stay in for the whole review. A large dildo gets asked to go all the way down to the base, or to be ridden in standing doggy. A chastity cage gets locked on, on camera. A vibrator gets used until you cannot keep still. The job is what you were sent the toy for, so it can never be bought out of the brief.
  • The extras are chosen to suit that job rather than at random. A mouth test comes with lipstick and lashes; hands come with nails, rings and a bracelet; riding comes with heels and stockings; a cage comes with a vibrator used on it, and a sissygasm. That pairing is deliberate — an offer should read like something a person thought up.

Extras that name a category resolve to a real item from your collection with its photo and name, matched on the taxonomy category first and on the product name second, so a half-sorted catalogue still works. Where nothing fits, the generic wording stands.

Wardrobe and product extras can be bought out of a brief. The ones that are really the job — grinding on it, showing your tape, finishing on camera — cannot.

A catalogue without toys still plays

If your catalogue has no toys to offer — it is empty, you only have wardrobe in it, or every toy you own is already on a shelf or in the inbox — the game falls back to built-in sample stock so the shop is never left with nothing to do. Samples cover one of each toy kind plus a small wardrobe for the briefs to name. They are marked everywhere they appear, they carry no photos, and the shop shows a line pointing at your catalogue. Fill it and the brands go back to offering your own things.

Extras always prefer your real collection, even when the toy being tested is a sample — those are your own clothes.

The inbox is topped up when you open the shop, when you clear an offer (turning it down or paying it off) and when you deliver a test, so you can never empty it and get stuck.

Each offer carries one to three briefs — conditions the brand wants met on camera. Briefs that name a product category resolve to a real item from your collection, with its photo and name; if that category is empty, the generic wording stands.

What you can do Cost Effect Film it — Opens the shoot; needs a free shelf Turn down 6 standing The offer is gone Pay it off 40 The offer is gone and your standing holds Drop a brief 60 Removes one wardrobe or product condition, cuts the required footage by a third and the fee by a fifth

Your standing (0–100, starts at 50) decides how many offers wait for you and how well they pay. Under 30 the inbox thins to two; over 70 it runs to six and the fees are roughly triple what they were at the bottom. Delivering a test adds 4.

Offers expire three days after they arrive.

docs.title: Filming
docs.text:
The shoot is a full-screen camera with the brief pinned in the corner as a shot list you tick off, and a counter showing how much footage you have against what was asked.

Nothing records until you press Record. From there you can hold the take with Pause and pick it back up; the counter only runs while the camera does, so it always reads as footage shot rather than time spent on the screen. The recording uploads to the server in five-second chunks while you film, so nothing is held in the browser; when you wrap, the server repairs the container and cuts a thumbnail.

There are three ways to make the review, picked on the shoot screen itself:

Source How it works This camera The webcam on the machine you are playing on. The camera picker at the bottom lists everything available My phone Scan the QR with your phone; its camera arrives over WebRTC as just another entry in that picker, and is selected for you the moment it connects. This works even when you refused the laptop camera — the phone can be the only camera you have A file A video you already filmed. It takes the place of the recording — nothing is captured here, and its own length counts as the review length

Whichever you use, the rest is identical: the file is finalized, a thumbnail is cut, and the product goes on the shelf with the review attached.

You can stop early. Short reviews simply sell worse — and if you deliver under 60% of the requested footage, a quarter of that listing's commission is clawed back as returns.

docs.title: How things sell
docs.text:
Every day you close, each listing draws visitors and converts a fraction of them.

visitors   = shop traffic × freshness × campaign
conversion = 10% × price factor × review factor    (capped at 35%)
sales      = visitors × conversion
you get    = sales × asking price × your cut
Term What drives it Shop traffic 40 visitors, plus 25 per shop level above the first Freshness Full on its first day, three quarters on the second, half after that Price factor Asking under the catalogue price sells faster, over it slower (0.3–2.0) Review factor 0.4 at nothing filmed, 1.0 at the full requested length, plus 0.2 if every brief was met Campaign A bought campaign multiplies traffic by a roll between 0.8 and 2.2 — it can flop

There is deliberately no floor under the conversion rate: a listing nobody would buy sells nothing. Asking prices are held between a quarter and triple the catalogue price, because outside that band the price lever would beat every other decision in the game.

Products without a price in your catalogue fall back to the median of their category, then to a flat 35.

docs.title: The settlement
docs.text:
Opening the shop closes the books and prints a receipt: every listing's sales and commission, any returns, the shelf rent, and what it came to. Rent is 8 per occupied shelf per day, so a shelf holding something that does not sell costs you money.

Listings run for 3 days and then come off the shelf into the archive, where their page and review stay readable until you delete them.

docs.title: Spending
docs.text: Upgrade Steps Prices Shelves 3 → 7 150 · 400 · 900 · 2000 Your cut 8% → 11% → 14% → 17% → 20% 250 · 600 · 1200 · 2500 Shop size Level 1 → 5 (more visitors per listing) 500 · 1500 · 4000 · 9000 Campaign Per listing, per day A tenth of the catalogue price, minimum 25

docs.title: Your reviews
docs.text:
The Reviews section holds every review this shop has filmed — the ones on the shelf and the ones whose listing has run out. Each one plays back in place, and carries what it sold and whether the brief was met.

From here a review can be exported to your video collection: give it a name, add tags and pick actors, and it goes through the normal video import as a job. The shop keeps its own copy, so the product page still plays it. A review whose listing has run out can also be deleted here, file and all.

docs.title: The product page
docs.text:
Every listing gets a real storefront page: the product's own photo and price from your catalogue, your recorded review, and the customer reviews underneath. It is the one bright screen in the game — the rest of the shop is the back office — and it stays readable after the listing expires.

Customers write according to how the review was filmed and how it was priced, and now and then one asks for something else to be tested next.

docs.title: Where it is stored
docs.text: The shop is JSON on the player's UserGameSettings row, exactly like OnlyCams keeps its profile; a shoot is a GameSession. Both tables already existed, so this game needed no schema change. Review recordings live in normal file storage and can be deleted per listing from the archive.

docs.title: Game bundles
docs.text:
A game bundle is a content pack for one arcade game — extra levels you load once and keep. Think of it as a season of a show rather than a save file: it arrives finished, it plays immediately, and you can take it off air again without losing it.

Bundles live on the Arcade page, under the Bundles tab — every pack belongs to a game, so the place you pick a game is the place you add more of them. The tab has two shelves: what is available to load, and what is already loaded.

docs.title: What is inside one
docs.text:
A bundle is a single .gerobundle file. Inside it:

Component Description Bundle info Name, tagline, description, cover art and which game it is for Game levels Fully configured levels — questions, answers, points, timers, score triggers and end screens Tags The tag names the levels filter on

That is the whole list, and the omissions are deliberate. A bundle brings no videos and no sources. Earlier versions created media subscriptions on import, which quietly added downloads you never asked for on the strength of a filter inside a quiz. A pack may name a tag — a tag holds nothing — but it does not get an opinion about what you download.

Bundles are portable: they reference tags by name rather than by id, so the same file works on any Gero installation.

docs.title: Loading one
docs.text:
Two ways in, both ending in the same place:

  • From the store — press check for new bundles on the Bundles tab, then load one from the Available shelf. This is the only moment Gero contacts the download server; the page itself is built from the last answer it got, so it opens instantly and works offline.
  • From a file — Import file on the Bundles tab, or the Bundle tab of the header's Import dialog. Pick a .gerobundle and it loads.

Loading a bundle:

  1. Creates any tags its filters name that your library does not have yet.
  2. Creates its levels, marked as belonging to that bundle.
  3. Saves its cover art.

Nothing is created halfway. A bundle that is wrong in any way is refused as a whole, because a half-loaded pack looks exactly like a successful one from the level list.

Loading the same version twice does nothing. Loading a newer version replaces the levels that bundle owns — anything you duplicated out of it is untouched.

docs.title: On air and off air
docs.text:
Every loaded bundle has a tally light. On air means its levels show up in the game. Off air means they do not — but nothing is deleted, nothing is renumbered, and switching it back on puts everything exactly where it was.

Use it to keep a pack you are not in the mood for without cluttering the level select.

Removing a bundle is the permanent version: the levels and their play history go with it. One exception — a level that a recorded gameplay points at is kept and becomes an ordinary level you can edit, so the recording does not lose the thing it was recorded from.

docs.title: Bundle levels are read-only
docs.text:
A level that came from a bundle carries the bundle's name on its card, and the editor opens it read-only.

That is not the app being precious. The bundle owns those levels: the next update of the pack replaces them, so an edit made in place would vanish without warning. Duplicate to edit — the copy is yours, fully editable, and untouched by anything the bundle does later.

In Quiz Time the level select gains a filter row once a bundle is loaded, so you can play Mine, one pack, or everything.

docs.title: Content that does not match
docs.text:
A bundle was written against somebody else's library. Its filters name tags that yours may simply not have.

Quiz Time no longer refuses to start over this. A question whose filter matches nothing plays random clips instead, and the preview screen says so before you begin — "question 3 has no clips matching its filter" — with a start anyway button. The only thing that still stops a level is an empty library, because then there is nothing to fall back on either.

The practical effect: tag your library the way the packs expect and the clips are relevant; do not, and the packs still play.

docs.title: Which games
docs.text:
Right now: Quiz Time.

The format has room for the rest — binary assets, and content that is not level-shaped — and the other games are being added one at a time, because each needs something different. Follow the Beat needs its audio and a beat profile; Obey needs a portrait for each persona; Dare deck's content is a pool of lines rather than levels at all.

A bundle that needs something this version cannot install says so and refuses, rather than loading the half it understands.

docs.title: A Legend perk
docs.text:
Bundles from the store are for Legend-tier patrons. Your supporter key is the same one the app uses to check for updates — paste it once in Settings → Updates and both work.

A key issued before bundles existed still works for updates but not for the store. If that is you, the supporter page will say so; generate a new key and paste it again.

docs.title: Gameplay recording
docs.text:
Gameplay recording captures a playthrough of an arcade game level exactly as it appears on the website — video and audio — and turns it into a publishable promo clip. The recording is produced by a background job and is driven entirely by the same React play pages a human plays, so what you validate by playing is what gets recorded.

Supported games: Quiz Time, Follow the Beat, and Caption Creator.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
Navigate to Gameplays → create new. The wizard has four steps; your progress is kept in the URL and a local draft, so a refresh or an accidental click-away never loses your work.

  1. Game + level — pick the game and the level to record.
  2. Recording settings — game-specific options:
    • Quiz Time: per question, choose which answer is given, how long the question stays on screen, and an optional pre-answer delay; plus background-music and fragment-audio volumes.
    • Follow the Beat: start-screen and end-screen durations and music volume.
  3. Post-process — optionally prepend an intro and/or append an outro. (Future actions such as auto promo-clip and custom thumbnail will appear here.)
  4. Review — confirm everything, then Generate.

Generating queues a job. The overview page shows an In progress section at the top; clicking an item opens the live job console with traces. Finished gameplays are listed below, filterable by game and level and sortable; clicking one opens its detail page.

docs.title: Raw vs. merged output
docs.text: The raw gameplay (without intro/outro) is always stored separately. When an intro/outro is configured, a merged final file is produced and shown on the detail page; the raw file is kept so you can change the intro/outro later and re-merge without re-recording. With no intro/outro, the detail page shows the raw file directly.

docs.title: How capture works
docs.text: The recorder drives a headless Chromium (Playwright) against the real play page in bot mode and records deterministically with a virtual clock (frame-by-frame), so output quality does not depend on host performance. Hardware encoding uses VA-API when /dev/dri/renderD128 is available, with a software fallback. An optional time-sharding mode renders segments in parallel to speed up long recordings.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Audio is reconstructed from a declarative audio plan the play page exposes in bot mode, expressed in the same logical timeline as the video frames. Because video and audio derive from one timeline, they stay in exact sync by construction — no drift, no early/late jumps. The plan carries every track with its start/stop, volume and fades, and (for Follow the Beat) per-segment playback-speed changes, which are rendered segment-by-segment so variable-speed soundtracks stay sample-accurate.

docs.title: Detail page
docs.text: The detail page shows the merged-or-raw player, a settings summary, durations and status, the job console, and publish controls: a published URL plus comments, and a publish/unpublish toggle. Changing the intro/outro re-runs the merge against the stored raw file. Delete is available in the danger zone.

docs.title: Media subscriptions
docs.text: Media subscriptions let you automatically download content from your favorite sources on a schedule. Think of it as an RSS feed for videos — set it up once, and Gero keeps your library fresh.

docs.title: Supported sources
docs.text:
Gero automatically detects the source type from the URL you provide:

Source Type Example RedGifs Animated clips Category or user pages PornHub Full videos Channel or category pages Shorts.XXX Short-form video Channel shorts feed Reddit Mixed Subreddit listings and user profiles xHamster Short-form video Shorts search, creator or user shorts tab

More sources may be added in future updates.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Each subscription can run on its own schedule:

Schedule Frequency Manual Only runs when you trigger it Hourly Checks every hour Daily Checks once per day Weekly Checks once per week Monthly Checks once per month

You can enable or disable individual subscriptions without deleting them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create a subscription — Paste a source URL and pick a schedule
  2. Gero detects the type — The source type is determined automatically from the URL
  3. On each run — Gero fetches new content from the source (up to a configurable limit per run, default: 250)
  4. Each video is processed — Every downloaded video goes through the full import pipeline
  5. Tags and actors are linked — Auto-tagging extracts metadata from the source and matches against your existing tags
  6. History is logged — Every run is tracked so you can see what was imported and when

docs.title: Configuration options
docs.text: Setting Description URL The source page to fetch from Schedule How often to check for new content Is enabled Toggle on/off without deleting Max videos per run Limit how many videos to download per execution (default: 250) Tags Tags to automatically apply to all imported videos Actors Filter by specific actors

docs.title: Auto-tagging
docs.text:
You can link tags to a subscription. When Gero imports a video through that subscription, those tags are automatically applied in addition to any tags extracted from the source itself.

This is useful for categorizing content by subscription. For example, a subscription to a specific RedGifs category could auto-apply a "favorites" tag.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Every subscription run is logged with:

  • When it ran
  • How many videos were imported
  • Success or failure status

This gives you full visibility into what's being added to your library and when.

docs.title: Panic mode
docs.text: Panic mode instantly hides the entire app behind an innocent safe screen — a YouTube video of your choosing. Trigger it with a keyboard shortcut, or wire it to an external system (a smart doorbell, a camera, Home Assistant) so GERO hides itself the moment someone approaches.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When panic mode is triggered, GERO covers everything with your configured safe URL playing full-screen. Nothing of what you were doing is visible. You can trigger it two ways:

  • Keyboard shortcut — held with Ctrl + Shift plus a key you pick (default P)
  • Webhook — an HTTP request from any external system, which pops a confirm dialog (optionally with a live camera preview)

All settings live under Settings → Panic mode.

docs.title: 1. Enable it and set a safe URL
docs.text: Turn on Enable panic mode, then paste any YouTube URL into Safe URL. Watch, Shorts, and youtu.be links are automatically converted to embed format on save. Use Test preview to see exactly what the safe screen will look like.

docs.title: 2. Choose a keyboard shortcut
docs.text: The shortcut is always held with Ctrl + Shift. Click the key button to record a new one (default is P, i.e. Ctrl + Shift + P).

docs.title: 3. (Optional) Set up a webhook trigger
docs.text:
Panic mode generates a private webhook URL with a secret token. Any system that can send an HTTP POST can trigger it — Home Assistant, a door sensor, a UniFi camera, a doorbell, etc.

The JSON body accepts two optional fields:

Field Description source A label identifying which system triggered it (e.g. unifi-front-door) cameraUrl An optional camera URL shown as a live preview in the confirm dialog

Example payload:

{
  "source": "unifi-front-door",
  "cameraUrl": "rtsps://192.168.1.50:7441/abc?enableSrtp"
}

Regenerate the token if it leaks

The webhook URL contains a secret token. If it's ever exposed, hit Regenerate token in the settings — the old URL stops working immediately.

docs.title: Supported camera URL types
docs.text:
The optional camera preview understands:

  • HLS — .m3u8
  • Video files — .mp4, .webm
  • Snapshot images — .jpg, .png
  • RTSP / RTSPS — rtsp:// or rtsps://, transcoded to HLS server-side via FFmpeg (expect ~5–15 s latency)

Use Camera feed test in the settings to confirm a camera is reachable before relying on it during a real trigger.

docs.title: Example uses
docs.text:
• Quick privacy — a single Ctrl + Shift + P flips the screen to a normal-looking video the instant someone walks in
  • Smart doorbell — POST the webhook from your doorbell automation so GERO hides itself, with a live feed of who's at the door in the dialog
  • Home Assistant — trigger panic mode from any HA automation (motion sensor, presence detection, a dashboard button)

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: Tags are how Gero organizes and categorizes your content. They power the filtering, searching, and browsing experience across your entire library.

docs.title: Automatic tagging
docs.text:
When you import a video, Gero automatically extracts tags from:

  1. The source page — Tags, categories, and metadata from the original website (RedGifs, PornHub, YouTube, etc.)
  2. The video title — Gero compares the video name against all existing tags in your database
  3. Tag aliases — Alternative names you've defined for tags are also matched

This means your library organizes itself as it grows. The more tags you have, the smarter auto-tagging becomes.

docs.title: Manual tags
docs.text: You can always add or remove tags manually on any video or fragment. Tags are stored in lowercase and automatically deduplicated.

docs.title: Tag groups
docs.text:
Tag groups let you organize related tags into categories. For example:

Group Example tags Actions kiss, dance, run Locations beach, office, outdoor Mood romantic, intense, chill

Groups have a display order so you can control how they appear in the UI. Each tag can belong to one group.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Tags support aliases — alternative names that map to the same tag. For example, the tag compilatioon could have aliases like compilations or comps.

When Gero auto-tags a video, it checks both the tag name and all aliases for matches. This helps catch different naming conventions across sources.

You can set aliases as a comma-separated list when editing a tag.

docs.title: Verified tags
docs.text: Tags can be marked as verified to indicate they are curated and trustworthy. This is useful when your library has hundreds of auto-generated tags and you want to distinguish the ones you've personally reviewed.

docs.title: Tag-based filtering
docs.text:
Tags are used throughout the app for filtering:

  • Video library — Filter by one or more tags
  • Theater mode — Browse content matching specific tags
  • Media subscriptions — Auto-apply tags to downloaded content
  • Arcade games — Select content for games based on tags
  • Fragments — Tags are inherited from parent videos or added individually

docs.title: Videos
docs.text: Videos are the core of Gero. Everything starts with importing content into your library, where it gets processed, tagged, and made ready for viewing.

docs.title: Importing videos
docs.text: There are two ways to add videos to Gero:

docs.title: From a URL
docs.text: Paste a link from any site supported by yt-dlp (YouTube, RedGifs, PornHub, and thousands more). Gero downloads the video and processes it automatically.

docs.title: From a file
docs.text: Drop files into the watched folder (if configured). Supported formats include anything FFmpeg can handle: MP4, WebM, MKV, AVI, MOV, and more.

docs.title: Processing pipeline
docs.text:
When a video is imported, Gero runs it through a multi-step pipeline:

Step What happens Download Fetches the video from the URL (skipped for local files) Validate Verifies the file is a valid video Get metadata Extracts duration, codec info, and other technical details Optimize Re-encodes to a standard format if needed Convert Converts to a browser-friendly format (MP4/WebM) Generate thumbnail Creates a poster image for the video Generate preview Creates an animated preview clip Process tags Auto-extracts tags from the source (see Tags) Process actors Matches known actors by name Trigger fragments Queues automatic fragment generation

All processing runs as a background job with real-time progress tracking. You can continue using the app while videos are being processed.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
Fragments are short clips extracted from videos. Gero can auto-generate them or you can create them manually by setting start and end times.

Each fragment gets its own:

  • Thumbnail
  • Duration
  • Tags (inherited from parent video or added manually)

Fragments are the building blocks for Theater Mode browsing and the Arcade games — Follow the Beat, Caption Creator, and QuizTime all build their levels from your fragments.

docs.title: Theater mode
docs.text:
Theater Mode is a full-screen, TikTok/Reels-style player for browsing your content.

Desktop controls:

  • Scroll up/down to navigate between videos
  • Click the scrubber to seek
  • Arrow keys to navigate
  • Space to play/pause
  • M to mute/unmute

Mobile controls:

  • Swipe up/down to change videos
  • Tap to play/pause
  • Double-tap to seek forward/backward

docs.title: Review system
docs.text:
New videos and fragments are marked as unreviewed by default. You can use the review system to:

  • Mark content as reviewed after checking quality
  • Hide videos you don't want to see in browsing
  • Show/unhide hidden content at any time

This helps you curate your collection, especially when importing large batches via media subscriptions.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actors represent people featured in your videos. During import, Gero automatically matches known actor names found in the video title. You can also manually link actors to videos.

Each actor can have:

  • A profile picture
  • Birth date and origin info
  • Links to all their videos

Use actors to filter and browse your collection by performer.

docs.title: Android app
docs.text:
Gero ships as a real Android app — not a browser shortcut. It's the same interface you use on the desktop, packaged into an APK, talking to your own server.

Nothing about it is hosted by us. The app is an empty shell until you point it at your Gero instance.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
1. Open the supporter portal and sign in with Patreon
  2. Go to Installers and pick the newest release
  3. Download gero-android-<version>.apk — it sits next to the Windows zip (the shared Dropbox folder still carries both)
  4. Open the file on your phone and confirm the install

Android will ask you to allow installs from your browser or file manager the first time — that permission is per-app and only needs granting once.

Updating

Install a newer APK straight over the old one. Your server address and settings survive the update; there's no need to uninstall first.

Matching versions

The APK in a version folder is built from the same commit as the Windows build beside it, so keeping both on the same version is the safe default.

docs.title: First run: pointing it at your server
docs.text:
On first launch the app asks for your server address. Enter the same URL you'd use in a browser on that network, including the port:

http://192.168.1.20:8080

The scheme is optional — leave out http:// and the app adds it. A trailing slash is stripped for you.

The app then asks your server for its configuration and, if that succeeds, drops you straight into Gero. From then on it starts there directly.

Field Example Notes Server address http://192.168.1.20:8080 LAN address, hostname or a public URL Port :8080 Required unless your server runs on 80/443

docs.title: Changing the server later
docs.text: Go to Settings → App server. You can test a new address, save it, or clear the stored one to get the setup screen back — useful if you move between a LAN address at home and a remote address elsewhere.

docs.title: When it says the server is unreachable
docs.text:
The most common causes, in order:

Cause Fix Wrong network The phone must be able to reach the server. On Wi-Fi at home that means the same network; over mobile data you need a publicly reachable address or a VPN Missing port 192.168.1.20 is not the same as 192.168.1.20:8080 Server bound to localhost Gero must listen on the machine's LAN address, not only 127.0.0.1 Firewall Windows Firewall blocks inbound connections on the Gero port by default — allow it Older Gero version The app asks the server for its config. Servers older than 2.2.0 may not answer; update the server

Tip

Test the exact address in your phone's browser first. If it doesn't load there, the app can't reach it either — that separates a network problem from an app problem.

docs.title: What's different from the browser
docs.text:
• The back button navigates back through the app instead of closing it. From the home screen it exits, as Android expects
  • Games run fullscreen, without the browser's own chrome eating the top of the screen
  • The status bar matches the app's theme rather than the browser's
  • The interface is the same one the desktop serves, so anything you can do in the browser you can do here

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text: The app is a Capacitor shell around Gero's React interface. Every push that touches the web project rebuilds it, so the APK never lags behind the server release it's meant to run against.

docs.title: Browser extension
docs.text: The Gero browser extension lets you import videos, audio tracks, and create media subscriptions directly from any webpage. Available for Chrome and Firefox.

docs.title: Chrome installation
docs.text:
1. Download the latest extension files from the Dropbox folder (or the src/Web.Extension/chrome/ folder if building from source)
  2. Open Chrome and navigate to chrome://extensions/
  3. Enable Developer mode using the toggle in the top-right corner
  4. Click Load unpacked
  5. Select the chrome/ folder containing the extension files
  6. The Gero icon appears in your toolbar — click it to open the popup

Pin the extension

After installing, click the puzzle piece icon () in Chrome's toolbar and pin Gero for quick access.

docs.title: Firefox installation
docs.text:
1. Download the latest extension files from the Dropbox folder (or the src/Web.Extension/firefox/ folder if building from source)
  2. Open Firefox and navigate to about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox
  3. Click Load Temporary Add-on...
  4. Select any file inside the firefox/ folder (e.g., manifest.json)
  5. The Gero icon appears in your toolbar

Temporary add-on

Firefox temporary add-ons are removed when the browser closes. For persistent installation, the extension needs to be signed and distributed through Mozilla Add-ons (AMO).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
After installing, you need to point the extension to your Gero instance:

  1. Click the Gero extension icon in your toolbar
  2. Click the gear icon () to open settings
  3. Set the API URL to your Gero address — the URL shown in the Gero app window (default http://localhost:9710)
  4. Set the Web app URL to the same address (on the Windows build the web UI is served by the API, so they're identical)
  5. Click Save

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
From 2.4.0 the extension signs in, so everything it imports belongs to your account rather than to nobody.

After saving the API URL, the popup shows a login screen: use the same email and password you use in Gero itself. It stays signed in and refreshes its own session, so this is a one-time step per browser — you only see it again if you sign out or change the API URL.

Upgrading from an older extension

Existing installs will ask you to sign in once after the update. Nothing you imported before is affected.

The status indicator at the top of the popup shows the connection state:

  • Green — Connected to the API
  • Red — Cannot reach the API

Default URL

On the standard Windows install Gero runs on http://localhost:9710 — use that for both the API and web app URL. If your app window shows a different address (or you run Gero on another machine), use that instead.

docs.title: Popup
docs.text:
Click the extension icon to open the popup. The current page URL is automatically filled in.

Choose what to import:

Action Description Video Import a video via yt-dlp. Optionally set a custom name. Audio Import an audio track. Optionally set title, artist, and category. Subscription Create a media subscription to monitor the URL for new content. Set a schedule and optional description.

Click the import button and wait for the confirmation message.

docs.title: Context menu
docs.text:
Right-click any page or link to access Gero actions:

  • Import video — sends the page or link URL to Gero for video import
  • Import audio — sends the URL for audio track import
  • Add media subscription — creates a subscription for the URL

The extension shows a desktop notification when the action completes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution Status indicator is red Check that your Gero API is running and the API URL in settings is correct "Failed to fetch" errors Your browser may block requests to localhost with self-signed certificates. Visit the API URL directly in a new tab and accept the certificate Extension disappeared (Firefox) Temporary add-ons are removed on browser restart. Re-load the extension via about:debugging Import button stays loading Check the browser console (F12) for error details

docs.title: Step 1: Get access
docs.text:
Gero is distributed through Patreon. Subscribe to get access to download links:

  1. Go to patreon.com/geroappdev
  2. Subscribe to a tier that includes app access
  3. Log in with Patreon at the supporter downloads page — gero-downloads.geroappdev.workers.dev — and download the latest build (older versions stay available there too; a shared Dropbox folder also carries the builds)
  4. Optionally, generate an update key on that same page, so Gero can fetch later releases for you (see Updating)

One-time purchase

Once you download and install Gero, the app is yours forever. Even if you cancel your Patreon subscription, everything keeps working. You only miss new features and updates.

docs.title: Windows installation
docs.text: The easiest way to get started. The Windows build bundles everything you need: the API server, web UI, SQLite database, FFmpeg, and yt-dlp.

docs.title: Install steps
docs.text:
1. Download the latest Gero-x.x.x-win-x64.zip from the supporter portal (the shared Dropbox folder still carries it too)
  2. Extract the ZIP to a folder of your choice (e.g., C:\Gero)
  3. Run Gero.Startup.exe from the extracted folder
  4. Open your browser and navigate to the URL shown in the application window

That's it! Storage paths and other settings can be configured inside the app after first launch.

docs.title: The data folder
docs.text:
After first launch, Gero creates a data/ subfolder inside your installation directory. This is the most important folder in your installation:

C:\Gero\
├── api/                # API server — also serves the web UI from api/wwwroot
├── launcher/           # Launcher process
├── Gero.Startup.exe    # Entry point
└── data/               # ⚠️ Important!
    ├── storage/        # All your media files (videos, thumbnails, etc.)
    └── gero.db         # SQLite database with all your settings and metadata

Back up your data folder regularly

The data/ folder contains everything: your database, all media files, and configuration. If this folder is lost, your entire library is gone. Make regular backups of this folder to an external drive or cloud storage.

docs.title: Android app
docs.text: Gero also ships as an Android app that connects to the server you just installed. Install the server first, then see the Android app guide.

docs.title: Local analysis tools (Python)
docs.text:
Some of GERO's newer features analyse your library on your own machine and need a local Python with a couple of packages. This powers:

  • Analyse motion — measures the motion tempo of each clip (used by Follow the Beat to lock footage to the beat).
  • Audio / beat analysis — detects the beat of a song (also Follow the Beat).

Motion uses opencv-python-headless + numpy; audio uses librosa (plus an optional heavier beat-detection stack). GERO installs all of this for you.

You just need a Python with pip — GERO installs the analysis packages itself. opencv-python-headless, numpy and librosa are pulled in automatically the first time you run an Analyse motion or Analyse beats job. So if you already have Python (for example after upgrading), you don't re-download anything — just start the job and the script fetches what it needs.

If you don't have Python yet, open Settings → Tools and click Download Python: GERO downloads a self-contained Python (with pip). From then on the whole app always uses that local Python — nothing needs to be installed system-wide. While you're there, grab FFmpeg and yt-dlp too if they aren't set up yet.

Only fails when there's no Python at all

Analyse motion / Analyse beats only error with "Python executable not found" when GERO can't find any Python. Download it once from Settings (or have one on your PATH) and you're set — the packages install themselves on the first run.

This pairs with the AI models (vision + embeddings) from the Caption Creator & AI guide: motion + descriptions + embeddings together are what drive the smart clip-matching across the arcade.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
There are three ways to move to a newer version: copy the files over yourself, hand Gero a .zip you downloaded, or give Gero an update key and let it fetch the release for you.

Updating is a Windows desktop app feature. All three routes end the same way — Gero restarts and comes back on the new build, with your data/ folder untouched.

Gero never checks for updates on its own

There is no automatic update check. Gero doesn't check on a schedule, doesn't check at startup, and doesn't check in the background. It only asks whether a newer release exists when you press Check for updates yourself, and only if you've saved an update key. See the Privacy policy for exactly what that request contains.

ManualFrom a .zipWith an update key

The route that has always worked, and the one to use if the app won't start:

  1. Download the latest Gero-x.y.z-win-x64.zip from the supporter downloads page
  2. Close Gero if it's running
  3. Extract the ZIP to the same folder as your current installation (e.g., C:\Gero)
  4. When prompted, choose to replace all existing files
  5. Run Gero.Startup.exe to start the updated version

This is also the only route that can put you back on an older build, since the other two refuse anything that isn't newer.

Gero takes the .zip and handles the rest — no extracting, no overwriting, no closing Gero first.

  1. Download the latest Gero-x.y.z-win-x64.zip from the supporter downloads page
  2. Open Settings → Updates
  3. Choose Install from a file and pick the .zip you just downloaded
  4. Gero checks the package and tells you which version it will install
  5. Choose restart — Gero goes down, applies the update, and comes back on the new version

The restart is not optional, and not a formality: a running Gero can't overwrite its own files, so the update is staged to data/updates/ and applied by the bootstrapper on the way back up.

A staged update waits there until you restart, so you can pick it now and restart later. You can also cancel it before restarting and nothing changes.

The newest route, and the only one where you don't download anything by hand.

Set it up once

  1. Open the supporter downloads page at gero-downloads.geroappdev.workers.dev
  2. Log in with Patreon and generate an update key
  3. In Gero, go to Settings → Updates, paste the key and choose Save key

The key is stored encrypted on your own machine. It is never shown back to you — the Updates page only tells you whether a key is set.

Then, whenever you feel like it

  1. Open Settings → Updates and press Check for updates
  2. If there's nothing newer, Gero tells you that and stops there
  3. If there is, Gero shows you the version and its release notes, and asks you to confirm
  4. Confirm, and Gero downloads that release

From there it follows exactly the same path as installing from a .zip: the same validation, staged to data/updates/, applied on the next restart.

Nothing happens without you

The check only runs when you press the button, and the download only starts once you've accepted the version it found. Without a saved key the check can't run at all.

The in-app routes only accept a real, newer release

Whether the package came from your disk or from the download server, it is rejected unless it contains Gero.exe, api/Gero.Api.exe and a version.txt, and that version is strictly newer than the build you're running. That rules out the wrong zip, a half-downloaded one, and re-installing what you already have. It also means you can't roll back this way — for that, use the manual route.

The reminder on the homepage

If a check found a newer version and you haven't installed it, a quiet line appears on the homepage linking back to the updates page. That line is drawn from the stored result of the check you already ran — it does not start a new one.

Your data is safe

Updating only replaces the application files (api/, launcher/, Gero.Startup.exe, etc.). Your data/ folder with the database and media files is not overwritten — everything stays intact.

Database migrations run automatically on startup, so your data is always compatible with the new version.

Upgrading from a pre-React build? Remove the old web/ folder

Newer builds serve the web interface directly from the API (api/wwwroot) and no longer ship a separate web/ folder. Extracting an update on top of your existing install doesn't delete old files, so an unused web/ folder is left behind. Once you've started the new version and confirmed it works, you can safely remove it:

  1. Close Gero
  2. Open your install folder (e.g., C:\Gero)
  3. Delete the web/ folder
  4. Start Gero again with Gero.Startup.exe

Your data/ folder is never touched, so nothing of yours is at risk.
